Source: https://securelist.com/uefi-bootkit-blackx/121539/

The report describes a BlackX user-mode RAT using Google Drive, OneDrive and Yandex.Disk files as tasks. Hexadecimal filename suffixes select .NET execution, file upload and download; execution results and files are uploaded to storage. These fixtures reconstruct those operations, not original malware bytes. Suffixes, entry-point names and provider choices deliberately vary. Python fixtures model Python/.NET variants of the same task handlers; they are not claimed to be recovered Python malware.

Neutral capabilities retain notable criticality. The hostile channel requires cloud context, hexadecimal suffix comparisons and HTTP-sourced managed method invocation. File exfiltration additionally requires upload of local bytes selected by an HTTP response. C# queries bind the byte/path/body variables in adjacent statements; provenance rules trace nested calls in Python. These are source-local static relationships, not a proof of runtime reachability. The cloud context is same-file co-occurrence, not proof that every request targets that provider. Original binaries were unavailable. No assertion is made about matching compiled BlackX or an unprovided exploit implementation.

Positive cases: renamed.cs (OneDrive), drive_tasks.py (Google Drive), disk_tasks.py (Yandex.Disk). Partial attack cases local-backup.cs and different-body.cs retain the task channel but must not report remote-selected-file exfiltration. Benign cases retain relevant APIs/cloud references while removing execution, loading a different local buffer, overwriting the downloaded buffer, selecting a fixed local path, or putting the source inside a documentation string.

The article supplies no hostile file hashes or package coordinates. The feed value 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072 is a certificate serial. AF8A983B9ADA07EAE1259BF2953ABD40 identifies the legitimate jcef_helper.exe sideloading host. The hostile endpoint is www.archivetj.com. Scratch evidence preserves these identity distinctions and unsuccessful hash retrieval attempts.

Result-return coverage also supports direct C# HttpClient.PutAsync with StringContent(Convert.ToString(result)) and Python/.NET WebClient.UploadString(..., "PUT", str(result)). These neutral atoms bind the invocation result to the upload body. The result-return C2 composite requires HTTP-delivered assembly invocation and cloud-service context, independently of task suffix spelling; the original hexadecimal-suffix channel remains intact. Provider context remains same-file co-occurrence, not a fully resolved destination relationship.

Additional positive variants direct-results.cs and named-suffix-tasks.py use nonhexadecimal suffixes. Direct-unrelated-result.cs and the WebClient unrelated, overwritten and wrong-method controls reject mismatched bodies, reassignment and POST. The result-return rule must also remain absent from existing different-buffer.cs, overwritten-buffer.cs, documentation.cs and sync.cs controls. The code in these controls retains neutral reflection, transfer or cloud operations where relevant.

Coverage is source-level managed tasking. No detection is asserted for the unprovided Baton Drop exploit, callback/ETW manipulation, RC4 bundle layout, or native OxiDLLRunner/Rust loader. Nonhexadecimal variants receive result-return C2 coverage, but the separate cloud file-exfiltration composite retains its existing hexadecimal-suffix requirement.
